name: Bianca Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and out to the ewes before the kids are awake. We rent 95 hectares off the Ashcombe estate: about 220 ewes, a dozen suckler cows and spring barley on the flatter fields. Mornings are feeding and checking feet, afternoons are whatever broke overnight, usually something on the old 1998 Massey Ferguson. My partner Luc works on the council road crew, so I do the school run in the farm truck with sheep muck still on my boots.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love lambing, even the nights, because you feel useful in a way nothing else gives me. What wears me out is the money: the rent goes up every three years and the lamb price does whatever it likes. We have less than a month of bills put by, and every letter from the estate office makes my stomach turn. I keep the lambing records in a paper notebook, and I've never touched any of these AI apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch meeting: the problem was never computers, it's who owns the land and who sets the prices. I'd probably post that on the branch group too, because people forget it. Joan from next door would agree with me over the fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now. The rent review is due in 2027 and I already know it's going up. Hype or no hype, I'm one bad lambing away from the overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way we do: lambing in March, barley in by April, sell the store lambs at the autumn market. I'd push the union harder on the tenancy rules, because that's where I can make a difference. And I'd keep shopping at the discount store and skip the holiday again, same as this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same knot in my stomach I've had for ten years, just with nothing new added to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad lambing from the overdraft. What would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tractor repairs, every time. You can't skip the mortgage and you can't skip feeding sheep, so the Massey gets patched with wire and I hope it lasts. Last winter Luc welded the loader bracket himself in the yard at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elise and Theo about the farm in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids the farm is hard work and they don't owe it anything. Elise loves the lambs, but I won't let her think she has to stay. Theo just wants to drive the quad bike.

say: The real problem is **who owns the land**, not computers.
Farmers need the **union** pushing on rents and fair prices, whatever happens with AI.
think: Nothing changes, so my life stays **as hard as now**, with a rent rise coming in 2027.
I'm **one bad lambing** away from the overdraft, AI or no AI.
do: **Keep lambing** and selling store lambs at the autumn market as usual.
Push the **union branch** to campaign on tenancy rules before the 2027 rent review.
Skip the **family holiday** again and keep shopping at the discount store.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, carrying the same money knot she's had for ten years.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, I'm one bad lambing away from the overdraft.
fieldNote: Her worry is **rent and prices**, not technology; AI barely enters her picture of the plateau.
She turns straight to **the union** as the place where she has any power.
The **old tractor** held together with welding is her clearest sign of how thin the money is.

steps.text: Lamb in March and sell store lambs at the autumn market
Lobby the union branch on tenancy rules before the 2027 rent review
Skip the summer holiday and keep tractor repairs to home welding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs getting hit first, and farmers will be told to be grateful we're safe for now. I'd remind people at the branch that the big operators will grab the new machines first. I'd say we need rules on who gets to own these robots before they reach the fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't do much thinking work that a computer could take, so my hands are safe for a while. But the estate office could run the tenancies on software and squeeze us harder. And Luc's depot has a whole planning office that could shrink, which worries me for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still refuse to buy any of the apps; I'd rather pay Joan's son to show me once if the market forces me. I'd get the union to set up a meeting on what the estate is planning. And I'd start putting twenty a week into a tin, because that's all we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry that the people who caused none of this always end up paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Luc's depot. What exactly worries you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc's on the gritting lorry and the pothole crew, so his hands are needed. But the scheduling and the overtime decisions come from that office, and if a program decides the rota, the overtime goes first. Overtime is what pays for school shoes in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never buy the apps. What if the auction mart goes fully online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be stuck, wouldn't I? I'd go to the mart office and make the girl at the desk do it with me, and I'd complain about it the whole time. I'm not proud, just stubborn.

say: Office jobs get hit first, and farmers get told to be **grateful** for now.
We need **rules on who owns** the robots before they reach the fields.
think: My own hands-on work is **safe for a while**, but the estate could squeeze tenants with software.
Luc's **overtime** could vanish if a program sets the depot rota.
do: Ask the **union** to hold a meeting about the estate's plans.
Put **twenty a week** into a tin as a small cushion.
Refuse the apps unless the **auction mart** forces her online.
feel: **Uneasy**, and **angry** that people who caused none of it end up paying.
S1.quote: Overtime is what pays for school shoes in our house.
fieldNote: She sees the **household risk** through her partner's overtime, not her own job.
Her resistance to apps is **stubbornness she names herself**, not fear of the technology.
Saving twenty a week shows **how little room** there is to move.

steps.text: Get the union branch to call a meeting on the estate's plans
Put twenty a week into a tin for emergencies
Hold off on any farm apps until the auction mart forces it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is exactly why we need the government to step in, with a proper income guarantee for people on the land. I'd be on the branch group every night. I'd say the robots should belong to co-ops, not to the Ashcombe estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the estate would wait for the robots in 2031 and then not renew our tenancy. Why rent to a family when a machine can run the sheep for the land agent? The thinking side of my job is tiny, so 2028 hardly touches me, but 2031 is the end of the farm for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the union to fight for longer tenancy terms right away, before the robots come. I'd sell the suckler cows to clear the overdraft and stop paying for anything that isn't food or mortgage. I'd sit down with Luc and work out whether we could live on his wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly frightened. Three years sounds like a lot until you know the lease runs out in four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luc that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we've got three years before the robots, and we'd better spend them making a fuss. Then I'd probably cry in the lambing shed where the kids can't hear. Luc would make tea and say we've survived worse, which isn't true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your own work, given the warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd have to learn what these robots actually do, which I hate saying. Not to use one, but so I can argue with the land agent and not look stupid. Knowing your enemy, my gran called it.

say: The government must give people on the land a proper **income guarantee**.
The robots should belong to **farm co-ops**, not to the Ashcombe estate.
think: The estate will wait for **robots in 2031**, then refuse to renew the tenancy.
Thinking AI in 2028 hardly touches me, but **2031 ends the farm** for us.
do: Push the union for **longer tenancy terms** before robots arrive.
Sell the **suckler cows** to clear the overdraft.
Work out with Luc whether they can live on **his wage alone**.
feel: **Properly frightened**, counting the years between the robots and the lease ending.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a lot until you know the lease runs out in four.
fieldNote: She does her own sum: **thinking AI barely matters**, robots in 2031 decide everything.
Her fear is about the **landlord's choice**, not about robots doing the work badly.
She'd learn about robots only **to argue**, never to use one.

steps.text: Campaign through the union for longer tenancy terms this year
Write to her MP asking for an income guarantee for farm workers
Sell the twelve suckler cows to clear the overdraft
Cut spending to food, mortgage and feed only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to write proper laws if politicians bother. I'd say it at the branch, at the school gate and at the mart cafe. People would nod and then go home and do nothing, which is the usual way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same ending as the fast one, just with the robots around 2034. That's after our lease renewal in 2030, so we'd probably get one more term. One more term buys time for the kids to finish school here, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still sell the cows, but more slowly, a few each autumn. I'd get on the union's tenancy committee instead of just going to meetings. And I'd ask Luc to put his name down for the road crew supervisor course, because a supervisor keeps his job longer when the machines come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but I can breathe. There's a difference between a cliff and a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra years change for Elise and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elise would be sixteen by 2030, so she could finish her exams at the same school. Theo would still be small, but at least we wouldn't be moving him mid-year. Mostly I'd want them out of here before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you won't use any of it. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If Joan uses a robot shepherd and it works, I'd have to look at it. I'm stubborn, not daft.

say: Five years is enough to write **proper laws**, if politicians bother.
People will **nod and do nothing**, as they usually do.
think: Robots around 2034 come after the **2030 lease renewal**, so we likely get one more term.
The extra term lets the **kids finish school** in the village.
do: Sell the suckler cows **a few each autumn** rather than all at once.
Join the union's **tenancy committee** instead of just attending meetings.
Ask Luc to take the **road crew supervisor** course.
feel: **Still scared** but able to breathe, like facing a steep hill instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: There's a difference between a cliff and a steep hill.
fieldNote: She measures time in **lease terms** and school years, not in technology dates.
Even with time, she expects to **lose the tenancy** once robots arrive.
She admits she might try a robot **if her neighbour's works**, a crack in her resistance.

steps.text: Join the union's tenancy committee within six months
Sell three or four suckler cows each autumn
Get Luc onto the road crew supervisor course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say we have no excuse not to plan this properly, as a country. I'd be saying land should go to the people who work it. I'd probably write a letter to the local paper, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 means I'd be 56. That's late enough that I might farm most of my working life and then be pushed out at the end. It's not great, but it's a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm going as it is and stop panicking. I'd put the kids' future first: Elise to college, Theo to whatever he likes. I'd stay on the union committee and push for a fund that helps tenant farmers buy their land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly the old worries again. Rent and lamb prices will bother me more than robots for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at retraining in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in my fifties, so I doubt it. I'd sooner learn to fix the robots' fences than learn to be a programmer. Maybe I'd do some shearing for others as extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A right to buy the land I've farmed for fifteen years, at a fair price. With that I'd have something to sell, or to hand on. Without a right to buy the land, I'm a tenant till the day they don't want me.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuse** not to plan properly as a country.
Land should go to the **people who work it**.
think: Robots in 2039 arrive when I'm **56**, near the end of my farming life.
**Rent and lamb prices** stay my bigger worry for most of the decade.
do: **Keep farming** as now and stop panicking about robots.
Push the union for a **land purchase fund** for tenant farmers.
Take on **shearing work** for neighbours as extra money.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the old money worries outweighing the new ones.
S4.quote: Without a right to buy the land, I'm a tenant till the day they don't want me.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts her **from fear to planning**, but the tenancy worry stays.
Her wish is concrete: a **right to buy** at a fair price.
She'd rather do **shearing for cash** than retrain for a desk job.

steps.text: Keep the flock and barley going without big changes
Campaign in the union for a tenant land purchase fund
Take paid shearing jobs for neighbours each summer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because the robots would come before our lease is up and the estate would choose the machine. What would help is a right to buy the land we farm, or at least long tenancies the landlord can't break for a robot. I want somebody to write down that people who work the land count.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots, and that's the whole question. If the farmers owned them together, I'd even be glad of help at lambing. The machines are not my enemy; the landlord who buys them is.

headlineQuote: The machines are not my enemy; the landlord who buys them is.
portrait: Bianca, 43, rents a **95-hectare** sheep and barley farm from a big estate with her partner Luc.
She has under a month of savings, an **old tractor**, and never uses AI tools.
Her politics run through **the union**, and she blames landowners and prices, not machines.
She stays **anxious** in mild worlds and becomes **alarmed** when robots arrive before her lease ends.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 would come before her lease ends and the estate would choose them.
whatWouldHelp: A **right to buy** the land she farms, or long tenancies that can't be broken for a robot.
